analysis_steps.goal: Assess model sensitivity and parameter uncertainties via grid calculations and derive region gas masses

method.value: Run two independent grids of LIME models for the inner (125 models) and intermediate (750 models) regions, convolve with ALMA beams, rank by sum of squared residuals against the best model in 5 apertures for CO v=0 J=2-1 and v=1 J=3-2, visually inspect top-ranked models, and integrate density profiles to obtain gas masses.

findings_qualitative.value: The velocity field of the gas seen in absorption against the stellar disc in Band 7 is non-uniform across the disc, showing stronger absorption and an additional blue-shifted outflow component (up to ~15 km/s) towards the east compared to the west.

evidence.quote: The Band 7 observations also reveal that the spatial distribution of the absorption is not uniform against the stellar disc (Fig. 4).
For the CO v = 1, J = 3 - 2 line, a blue-shifted component seen towards the east has no counterpart above the noise level in the spectra extracted from the west.

findings_qualitative.value: No evidence is found in the CO data for a circumstellar disc around R Dor.

evidence.quote: We find no evidence in the data examined by us of a disk around R Dor, as suggested by (Homan et al. 2018).

findings_qualitative.value: The vast majority of the gas in the innermost layer (1.0 to 1.6 R_887um^*) is gravitationally bound and will fall back to the star or remain in the extended atmosphere for hundreds of years, while the transition at 1.6 R_887um^* marks the onset of the wind.

evidence.quote: If the current gas density distribution is representative of the inner circumstellar environment of R Dor, these values suggest that the vast majority of gas in the innermost region would fall back to the star or remain in the extended atmosphere for hundreds of years, while a significant fraction (or even all) of the mass in the intermediate region would be expelled. Therefore, our circumstellar model is consistent with the transition between the inner and intermediate regions (at 1.6 R_887um^*) corresponding to the transition between extended atmosphere and wind.

claims.hypothesis: The gas in the extended atmosphere of R Dor is stratified into distinct kinematic layers with non-spherical asymmetries between the near and far hemispheres.
claims.experiment: Analyse spatially resolved ALMA Band 6 and Band 7 absorption and emission line profiles of 12CO (v=0 J=2-1, v=1 J=2-1, v=1 J=3-2) and 13CO (v=0 J=3-2) and model them in 3D using LIME.
claims.result: In the near-side hemisphere, the innermost layer (1.0-1.6 R_887um^*) is infalling at <= 6 km/s while the intermediate layer (1.6-5.0 R_887um^*) is outflowing up to 13 km/s; reproducing the full emission line profiles requires reversing this velocity pattern in the far-side hemisphere.
claims.finding: The extended atmosphere exhibits large-scale convective and pulsation-driven velocity asymmetries, with opposite average radial motions between the near and far hemispheres in the inner and intermediate layers.

evidence.quote: By analysing the absorption against the star, we infer that the innermost layer in the near-side hemisphere is mostly falling towards the star, while gas in the layer above that seems to be mostly outflowing.
Our fits to the line profiles require the velocity distribution on the far side of the envelope to be on average mirrored with respect to that on the near side.

claims.hypothesis: The gas density and temperature profiles close to R Dor are very steep before transitioning to the large-scale wind.
claims.experiment: Fit multi-aperture spectra (45 to 240 mas) of four CO transitions with a three-zone power-law model in LIME and evaluate parameter uncertainties using model grids.
claims.result: The inner layer (1.0-1.6 R_887um^*) requires n_0 = 3.5e11 cm^-3 with power-law index eta = 7.0 and temperature index epsilon = 2.0 (containing ~3e-5 M_sun), transitioning at 1.6 R_887um^* to shallower slopes (eta = 2.8, epsilon = 0.73) with mass ~1.4e-6 M_sun consistent with the outer wind mass-loss rate.
claims.finding: Very efficient cooling and steep density gradients occur within 1.6 R_887um^* (the gravitationally bound extended atmosphere), beyond which the envelope transitions to the outflow.

evidence.quote: The gas temperature and density distributions have to be very steep close to the star to fit the observed emission and absorption, but become shallower for radii larger than ~ 1.6 times the stellar sub-mm radius.

While the gas mass in the innermost region is hundreds of times larger than the mass lost on average by R Dor per pulsation cycle, the gas densities just above this region are consistent with those expected based on the mass-loss rate and expansion velocity of the large-scale outflow.

claims.hypothesis: The stochastic velocity dispersion in the large-scale outflow of R Dor can be directly constrained from the narrow terminal-velocity absorption feature seen against the stellar continuum.
claims.experiment: Isolate the sharp absorption feature at 1.9 km/s in the 45 mas CO v = 0, J = 2 - 1 spectrum under two extreme baseline interpolation assumptions and fit Gaussian profiles.
claims.result: The fitted Gaussian standard deviations are 0.43 km/s and 0.32 km/s for the two scenarios.
claims.finding: The combined thermal and stochastic velocity standard deviation in the large-scale outflow is at most ~0.4 km/s.

evidence.quote: Using a sharp absorption feature seen in the CO v = 0, J = 2 - 1 line, we constrain the standard deviation of the stochastic velocity distribution in the large-scale outflow to be <= 0.4 km/s.

We find standard deviations for the gaussian functions of 0.43 and 0.32 km/s for scenarios i) and ii), respectively. The uncertainties on the derived values are at most at the 2% level. Hence, both scenarios imply a standard deviation of at most ~ 0.4 km/s.

claims.hypothesis: Discrete, dense, fast-moving gas blobs exist in the inner envelope of R Dor and account for the high-velocity emission wings.
claims.experiment: Extract CO v=0 J=2-1 and SO2 spectra towards two emission blobs (at ~0''.12 NW and ~0''.36 SE), derive SO2 rotational temperatures, locate the blobs via the model temperature profile, and compare their fluxes to the ACA high-velocity wings.
claims.result: Both blobs have gas masses of ~6e-8 M_sun, higher densities than the surrounding wind, and high radial expansion velocities (~13 km/s at ~3.4 R_887um^* for the inner blob; 16-28 km/s at 13.5-23.4 R_887um^* for the SE blob), and together with the extended atmosphere they account for all high-velocity emission seen in the ACA spectrum.
claims.finding: The high-velocity emission in R Dor is produced by the extended atmosphere and discrete ejected blobs rather than a global high-velocity wind acceleration, and blobs are likely decelerated by interaction with the slower wind on ~10 yr timescales.

evidence.quote: We characterise two blobs detected in the CO v = 0, J = 2 - 1 line and find densities substantially larger than those of the surrounding gas. The two blobs also display expansion velocities which are high relative to that of the large-scale outflow.
Hence, the combination of emission from the extended atmosphere and the high-velocity blob seem to account for all observed high-velocity emission detected in the ACA spectrum.

why_this_data.value: ALMA high angular resolution (~20-28 mas) spatially resolves the stellar sub-mm photosphere (~62 mas) and probes the extended atmosphere where dust forms and the wind is accelerated, while ground and vibrationally excited CO and 13CO lines trace different density and temperature regimes.

evidence.quote: The high angular resolution provided by ALMA allow us to probe the crucial region where dust formation and growth take place.
The high angular resolution of the sub-mm maps allows for even the stellar photosphere to be spatially resolved.

why_this_method.value: 3D non-LTE radiative transfer in LIME coupled with CASA simalma visibility simulations accounts for sub-thermal excitation of v = 1 CO levels, optical depth effects, and spatial filtering of extended emission by the interferometer.

evidence.quote: Hence, we consider LTE for calculating the excitation of 13CO and non-LTE for calculating the excitation of CO, for which vibrationally excited lines are also observed.

It is essential in our modelling to take into account the effects of observing an extended source with an interferometer. Hence, we simulated how the the two lines with a large emission region, CO v = 0, J = 2 - 1 and 13CO v = 0, J = 3 - 2, would be seen by ALMA.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Higher optical depths instead of a steep temperature profile to explain strong absorption relative to emission (rejected because the four modelled transitions have very different optical depths and the maximum brightness temperature in the optically thick CO v=0 J=2-1 ring is ~450 K).

evidence.quote: Lines that are more optically thick in reality than in our models could increase the strength of absorption with respect to emission without the need to make the gas cooler.
However, two facts speak against even higher optical depths being responsible for the relatively strong absorption.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Significant density asymmetry with more gas along the line of sight to the star than offset from it to explain the strong absorption (disfavoured because it requires a special envelope configuration).

evidence.quote: Another alternative for the steep temperature profile is a significant asymmetry in the gas densities, with more gas present in lines of sight towards the star than offset from it.
Although we cannot rule out this scenario, we disfavour it at this point because it requires a specific configuration of the envelope.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Keplerian orbit or far-side infall for the high-velocity southeast blob (rejected because orbital velocity at 21.5 AU around a 1.3 M_sun star is only ~7 km/s vs ~14 km/s observed, and flow velocity becomes more negative with distance).

evidence.quote: The expected orbital velocities at 21.5 AU from a 1.3 M_sun star is ~ 7 km/s, considerably less than the observed velocity along the line of sight.
Given that the flow velocity gets more negative with increasing distance from the star, the explanation that the blob is moving away from R Dor (and towards us) is favoured.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Lower terminal expansion velocity (4.8 km/s) to reconcile the systemic velocity discrepancy between ACA emission (6.7 km/s) and absorption against the star (7.4 km/s) (rejected because it produces a too-narrow CO v=0 J=2-1 line compared to the ACA profile).

evidence.quote: A maximum expansion velocity of 4.8 km/s would lead to a consistent value of v_sys = 6.7 km/s both for the fit to the ACA line and the absorption feature. However, this would produce a too-narrow CO v = 0, J = 2 - 1 line in comparison to the profile obtained with the ACA.

limitations_admitted.value: Single transitions in the intermediate region (only CO v=0, J=2-1 detected) cannot break the degeneracy between density and temperature distributions in that zone.

evidence.quote: This single transition does not allow us to break the degeneracy between density and temperature distributions for the intermediate region.

limitations_admitted.value: The exact shape of the velocity profile and the boundary at 5.0 R_887um^* between the intermediate and outer regions are not strongly constrained and depend on model assumptions.

evidence.loc: 6.2. Model for the inner circumstellar envelope
evidence.quote: However, the position of this second interface is not well constrained, and its purpose is only to mark the transition in the velocity profile as discussed in Section 6.2.2.
Hence, the exact shape of the velocity profile in the intermediate and outer regions is not very well constrained and, especially in the outer region, depends strongly on our assumptions.

limitations_admitted.value: The division of the velocity field into near-side and far-side hemispheres with opposite radial velocities is only a rough approximation to a complex 3D velocity field.

evidence.quote: As discussed in Section 4.2, we see signatures of different velocity components in the absorption profile of the CO v = 1, J = 3 - 2 line, which indicates that the far-side vs near-side division is only a rough approximation.

limitations_admitted.value: For both blobs, the SO2 excitation temperature might differ from the gas kinetic temperature, and the kinetic temperature inside the denser blobs might differ from the surrounding model temperature profile used to infer their radial distances.

evidence.quote: Also, for both blobs the excitation temperature of SO2 might differ from the kinetic temperature, and the kinetic temperature within the blob might differ from that of the surrounding gas (and, hence, from our model) given the difference in density.

limitations_admitted.value: Band 6, Band 7, and ACA observations were obtained at different epochs (Oct 24 2017, Nov 9 2017, Jan 1 2018), so stellar variability may affect comparisons between lines.

evidence.quote: Since the 13CO v = 0, J = 3 - 2 line was observed about two weeks later than the CO v = 0, J = 2 - 1 one, this could be at least partly due to variability.

referee_caveats_inferred: Model selection relies heavily on visual ('by-eye') inspection of multi-aperture spectra rather than a formal statistical likelihood or automated optimization.
In the sensitivity grid analysis, temperature continuity across zone boundaries was relaxed, producing physically discontinuous profiles.

Inferring 3D line-of-sight positions of the blobs by matching their LTE SO2 excitation temperatures to the 1D spherically symmetric ambient CO kinetic temperature profile assumes thermal equilibrium and identical thermal structure inside overdense shocks/clumps.

data_public_as_stated.value: ALMA data from project IDs 2017.1.00191.S, 2017.1.00824.S, and 2017.1.00595.S retrieved from the ALMA archive.

evidence.quote: We recovered the cubes comprising the lines mentioned above from the products associated with the projects in the ALMA archive.
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA#2017.1.00191.S, ADS/JAO.ALMA#2017.1.00824.S, and ADS/JAO.ALMA#2017.1.00595.S.

products_in_archive.value: CO v = 0 and v = 1 J = 2 - 1 cubes and ACA cubes were obtained from archive products; Band 7 cubes were imaged from calibrated measurement sets provided by ESO.

evidence.quote: The CO v = 1, J = 3 - 2 and the 13CO v = 0, J = 3 - 2 lines were imaged using CASA 5.7 and the calibrated measurement sets provided by ESO. The CO v = 0 and v = 1 J = 2 - 1 line cubes were obtained from the ALMA archive.

missing_for_reproduction: LIME model input files and custom C functions defining the 3D asymmetric density, temperature, and velocity distributions.
Specific transitions, frequencies, upper state energies, and Einstein A-coefficients of the 8 SO2 lines used in the population diagrams.
CASA tclean and simalma execution scripts and imaging parameters (robust weighting, cell size, masking).
reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: ~10-50 GB (calibrated measurement sets for Band 6 and Band 7 long-baseline projects plus archival image cubes and ~875 LIME 3D radiative transfer model cubes)
reproducibility.score_reason: The physical parameterization of the 3-zone model (Table 1) and the grid ranges (Table 2) are explicitly tabulated, and the archival data are public with stated project IDs. However, the exact SO2 transitions used for the blob temperature analysis, the CASA imaging/simulation parameters, and the LIME setup scripts are omitted, and final model selection relies on subjective visual inspection.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: All three ALMA datasets are public in the archive, the analytical parameterization of the 3-zone envelope is fully specified in Table 1, and the main scientific outputs (stochastic velocity dispersion, inner/intermediate gas masses, steep temperature/density exponents, and blob temperatures/masses) are concrete numerical values.

methods_papers.why: 3D molecular excitation and radiative transfer code LIME
CO rovibrational and rotational collisional rate coefficients
Population diagram method used to derive SO2 excitation temperatures

companion_papers.why: Analyzed the same high-resolution ALMA data of R Dor to measure stellar rotation and reported the high-velocity feature in SiO
Analyzed the stellar continuum from the same Band 7 ALMA dataset to determine the stellar radius and brightness temperature at 887 um
Upcoming companion study comparing the dust content of the inner blob to the gas properties derived in this paper
